verses.33:11: He sets my feet in the stocks; He watches all my paths.'
verses.33:12: Behold, in this you are not right; I will answer you, for God is greater than mortal man.
verses.33:13: Why do you contend against Him, because He does not answer for any of His words?
verses.33:14: For God speaks in one way, and in two, though one does not perceive it.
verses.33:15: In a dream, a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls upon men, in slumberings upon the bed,
verses.33:16: then He opens the ears of men, and seals their instruction,
verses.33:17: in order to turn man from his deed, and to conceal pride from a man;
verses.33:18: He keeps back his soul from the Pit, and his life from passing away by the sword.
verses.33:19: A man is also reproved with pain upon his bed, with unceasing ache in the multitude of his bones,
verses.33:20: so that his life loathes bread, and his soul abhors choice food.
verses.33:21: His flesh wastes away out of sight, and his bones that were unseen are laid bare.
verses.33:22: Indeed, his soul draws near to the Pit, and his life to the bringers of death.
verses.33:23: If there is for him a messenger, a mediator, one among a thousand, to declare to man his uprightness,
verses.33:24: then He shows grace to him and says, 'Rescue him from descending into the Pit; I have found a ransom.'
verses.33:25: His flesh shall become fresher than in youth; he shall return to the days of his youthful vigor.
verses.33:26: When he prays to God, He will accept him; he shall behold His face with shouts of joy, and He will restore to mortal man his righteousness.
verses.33:27: He looks upon men and says, 'I have sinned and perverted what is right, and it did not profit me.'
verses.33:28: He has redeemed his soul from passing into the Pit, and his life shall look upon the light.
verses.33:29: Behold, God does all these things, twice, even three times, with a man,
verses.33:30: to turn back his soul from the Pit, that he may be enlightened with the light of the living.
verses.33:31: Pay heed, O Job, listen to me; keep silent, and I will speak.
verses.33:32: If you have words to say, answer me; speak, for I desire to justify you.
verses.33:33: If not, then listen to me; keep silent, and I will teach you wisdom."
verses.34:2: "Hear my words, you wise men, and give ear to me, you who have knowledge.
verses.34:3: For the ear examines words, and the palate tastes its food.
verses.34:4: Let us choose for ourselves what is right; let us discern among ourselves what is good.
verses.34:5: For Job has said, 'I am righteous, yet God has removed my justice.
verses.34:6: Should I lie against my own right? My wound is incurable, though I am without transgression.'
verses.34:7: What man is like Job, who drinks up derision like water,
verses.34:8: who travels in company with workers of iniquity, and walks with wicked men?
verses.34:9: For he has said, 'A man gains no profit by taking delight in God.'
verses.34:10: Therefore listen to me, you men of understanding: far be it from God to do wickedness, and from the Almighty to commit iniquity.
verses.34:11: For He repays a man for his work, and according to a man's way He brings it upon him.
verses.34:12: Of a truth, God will not act wickedly, nor will the Almighty pervert justice.
verses.34:13: Who gave Him charge over the earth? And who laid upon Him the entire world?
verses.34:14: If He should set His heart upon Himself, and gather to Himself His Spirit and His breath,
verses.34:15: all flesh would expire together, and mankind would return to dust.
verses.34:16: If you have understanding, hear this; give ear to the sound of my words.
verses.34:17: Shall one who hates justice govern? And will you condemn Him who is righteous and mighty?
verses.34:18: Should one say to a king, 'You are worthless,' or to nobles, 'You are wicked'?
verses.34:19: How much less to Him who shows no partiality to princes, nor favors the rich above the poor? For they are all the work of His hands.
verses.34:20: In a moment they die; at midnight the people are shaken and pass away, and the mighty are removed without a human hand.
verses.34:21: For His eyes are upon the ways of a man, and He beholds all his footsteps.
verses.34:22: There is no darkness, nor shadow of death, where workers of iniquity may conceal themselves.
verses.34:23: For He has no need to examine a man further, that he should go before God in judgment.
verses.34:24: He shatters mighty men without inquiry, and sets others in their place.
verses.34:25: Therefore He knows their works; He overthrows them in the night, and they are crushed.
verses.34:26: He strikes them down as wicked men in the sight of onlookers,
verses.34:27: because they turned back from following Him, and had no regard for any of His ways,
verses.34:28: so that they caused the cry of the poor to come before Him, and He hears the cry of the afflicted.
verses.34:29: When He grants quietness, who then can condemn? And when He hides His face, who can behold Him—whether concerning a nation or a man alike—
verses.34:30: so that a godless man should not reign, nor those who lay snares for the people.
verses.34:31: For has anyone said to God, 'I have borne chastisement; I will offend no more;
verses.34:32: what I do not see, You teach me; if I have done iniquity, I will do so no more'?
verses.34:33: Should He repay it according to your terms, because you reject it? For you must choose, and not I; therefore declare what you know.
verses.34:34: Men of understanding will say to me, and every wise man who hears me will say,
verses.34:35: 'Job speaks without knowledge, and his words are without insight.'
verses.34:36: Oh, that Job were tried to the very end, because his answers are like those of men of iniquity!
verses.34:37: For he adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands among us, and multiplies his words against God."
verses.35:2: "Do you consider this to be just, that you have said, 'My righteousness is more than that of God'?
verses.35:3: For you ask, 'What advantage is it to you? What profit shall I gain, more than if I had sinned?'
verses.35:4: I will answer you with words, and your companions with you.
verses.35:5: Look to the heavens and see; and behold the clouds, which are higher than you.
verses.35:6: If you sin, what do you accomplish against Him? And if your transgressions are multiplied, what do you do to Him?
verses.35:7: If you are righteous, what do you bestow upon Him? Or what does He receive from your hand?
verses.35:8: Your wickedness affects a man like yourself, and your righteousness a son of man.
verses.35:9: Because of the multitude of oppressions they cry out; they cry for help from the arm of the mighty.
verses.35:10: Yet no one says, 'Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night,
verses.35:11: who instructs us more than the beasts of the earth, and makes us wiser than the birds of the heavens?'
verses.35:12: There they cry out, yet He does not answer, because of the pride of evil men.
verses.35:13: Surely God will not listen to an empty cry, nor will the Almighty regard it.
verses.35:14: Although you say that you do not behold Him, yet the case is before Him; therefore wait for Him.
verses.35:15: And now, because His anger has not punished, nor has He taken great notice of arrogance,
verses.35:16: therefore Job opens his mouth in vain; he multiplies words without knowledge."
verses.36:2: "Wait a little for me, and I will make it known to you, for there are yet words on behalf of God.
verses.36:3: I will bring my knowledge from afar, and I will ascribe righteousness to my Maker.
verses.36:4: For indeed my words are not falsehood; one complete in knowledge is with you.
verses.36:5: Behold, God is mighty, yet He does not despise any; He is mighty in strength of heart.
verses.36:6: He does not keep the wicked alive, but grants justice to the afflicted.
verses.36:7: He does not withhold His eyes from the righteous, but with kings upon the throne He seats them forever, and they are exalted.
verses.36:8: And if they are bound in chains, caught in the cords of affliction,
verses.36:9: then He declares to them their deeds and their transgressions, that they have acted arrogantly.
verses.36:10: He also opens their ears to discipline, and commands that they turn back from iniquity.
verses.36:11: If they listen and serve Him, they shall fulfill their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasantness.
verses.36:12: But if they do not listen, they shall pass away by the sword, and expire without knowledge.
verses.36:13: But the godless in heart harbor wrath; they do not cry for help when He binds them.
verses.36:14: Their soul dies in youth, and their life ends among the cult prostitutes.
verses.36:15: He delivers the afflicted by his affliction, and opens their ear by oppression.
verses.36:16: Indeed, He also drew you out of the mouth of distress into a broad place where there is no confinement, and what was set upon your table was full of rich food.
verses.36:17: Yet you are full of the judgment of the wicked; judgment and justice lay hold upon you.
verses.36:18: Take heed lest wrath entice you under a blow, and do not let a great ransom turn you aside.
verses.36:19: Will your cry for help avail to keep you out of distress, or all the exertions of strength?
verses.36:20: Do not long for the night, when peoples are taken away in their place.
verses.36:21: Take heed; do not turn to iniquity, for you have chosen this rather than affliction.
verses.36:22: Behold, God is exalted in His might; who is an instructor like Him?
verses.36:23: Who has prescribed His way for Him, or who has said, 'You have done iniquity'?
verses.36:24: Remember to extol His work, of which men have sung.
verses.36:25: All mankind has looked upon it; mortal man beholds it from afar.
verses.36:26: Behold, God is great, and we do not know Him; the number of His years is unsearchable.
verses.36:27: For He draws up the drops of water; they distill as rain from His mist,
verses.36:28: which the clouds pour down and shower abundantly upon mankind.
verses.36:29: Indeed, can anyone understand the spreading of the clouds, or the thunderings of His pavilion?
verses.36:30: Behold, He spreads His lightning around Him, and covers the roots of the sea.
verses.36:31: For by these He judges the peoples; He provides food in abundance.
verses.36:32: He covers both hands with lightning, and charges it to strike the mark.
verses.36:33: Its thunder declares concerning Him, and the cattle also concerning the storm that rises."
verses.37:1: "At this my heart also quakes, and leaps out of its place.
verses.37:2: Listen closely to the raging of His voice, and the rumbling that goes forth from His mouth.
verses.37:3: Beneath all the heavens He lets it loose, and His lightning to the corners of the earth.
verses.37:4: In its wake a voice roars; He thunders with His voice of majesty, and He does not hold them back when His voice is heard.
verses.37:5: God thunders wondrously with His voice; He does great things that we cannot comprehend.
verses.37:6: For to the snow He says, 'Fall upon the earth,' and to the shower of rain, even the downpour of His mighty rains.
verses.37:7: He puts a seal upon the hand of every man, that all mankind may know His work.
verses.37:8: Then the beasts withdraw into their lairs, and abide in their dens.
verses.37:9: From its chamber comes the whirlwind, and cold from the scattering winds.
verses.37:10: By the breath of God He gives ice, and the breadth of the waters is frozen solid.
verses.37:11: He also loads the thick cloud with moisture; He scatters the cloud of His lightning.
verses.37:12: And it wheels round and round by His guidance, that they may do all that He commands them upon the face of the habitable earth.
verses.37:13: Whether for correction, or for His earth, or for lovingkindness, He brings it to pass.
verses.37:14: Give ear to this, O Job; stand still and contemplate the wondrous works of God.
verses.37:15: Do you know how God lays His charge upon them, and causes the lightning of His cloud to shine forth?
verses.37:16: Do you know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of Him who is complete in knowledge,
verses.37:17: you whose garments are hot when the earth lies still beneath the south wind?
verses.37:18: Can you, with Him, spread out the skies, firm as a cast mirror?
verses.37:19: Make known to us what we shall say to Him; we cannot draw up our case because of darkness.
verses.37:20: Shall it be told Him that I wish to speak? Would any man ask to be swallowed up?
verses.37:21: And now men cannot look upon the light when it shines brightly in the skies, after a wind has passed by and cleared them.
verses.37:22: From the north comes golden splendor; upon God is awesome majesty.
verses.37:23: As for the Almighty, we cannot find Him out; He is exalted in power, and He does not violate justice and abundant righteousness.
verses.37:24: Therefore men fear Him; He has no regard for any who are wise of heart."
verses.38:1: Then the LORD answered Job from the whirlwind and said:
verses.38:2: "Who is this who obscures counsel with words without knowledge?
verses.38:3: Gird up your loins now like a mighty man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me.
verses.38:4: Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Declare it, if you possess understanding.
verses.38:5: Who fixed its measurements—surely you know!—or who stretched the measuring line over it?
verses.38:6: Upon what were its bases sunk, or who laid its cornerstone,
verses.38:7: when the morning stars sang out together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?
verses.38:8: And who enclosed the sea with doors when it burst forth, issuing from the womb,
verses.38:9: when I appointed the cloud as its garment, and thick gloom as its swaddling band,
verses.38:10: when I prescribed My boundary for it, and set in place a bar and doors,
verses.38:11: and said, 'Thus far you shall come, and no farther; and here the swelling pride of your waves shall be halted'?
verses.38:12: Since your days began, have you commanded the morning, and caused the dawn to know its place,
verses.38:13: that it might take hold of the skirts of the earth, and the wicked be shaken out of it?
verses.38:14: It is transformed like clay beneath a seal, and they stand forth like a garment.
verses.38:15: From the wicked their light is withheld, and the uplifted arm is broken.
verses.38:16: Have you come to the springs of the sea, or walked about in the recesses of the deep?
verses.38:17: Have the gates of death been revealed to you, or have you beheld the gates of the shadow of death?
verses.38:18: Have you comprehended the expanses of the earth? Declare it, if you know all of it.
verses.38:19: Where is the way to where light dwells? And darkness—where is its place,
verses.38:20: that you might take it to its territory, and that you might discern the paths to its house?
verses.38:21: You know it, for you were born then, and the number of your days is great!
verses.38:22: Have you entered the storehouses of the snow, or have you beheld the storehouses of the hail,
verses.38:23: which I have kept in reserve for the time of distress, for the day of battle and war?
verses.38:24: By what way is the light distributed, and the east wind dispersed over the earth?
verses.38:25: Who has cleft a channel for the pouring flood, or a path for the thunderbolt,
verses.38:26: to send rain upon a land where there is no man, upon a wilderness in which no mortal is,
verses.38:27: to satisfy the waste and desolate ground, and to cause the shoots of tender grass to spring forth?
verses.38:28: Does the rain have a father? Or who has fathered the drops of dew?
verses.38:29: From whose womb did the ice come forth? And the frost of heaven—who gave birth to it?
verses.38:30: The waters become concealed like stone, and the face of the deep is locked fast together.
verses.38:31: Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades, or loosen the cords of Orion?
verses.38:32: Can you lead forth the Mazzaroth in their season, or guide the Bear with her children?
verses.38:33: Do you know the statutes of the heavens, or can you establish their dominion upon the earth?
verses.38:34: Can you lift up your voice to the clouds, so that an abundance of waters may cover you?
verses.38:35: Can you send forth lightnings, that they may go and say to you, 'Here we are'?
verses.38:36: Who has placed wisdom in the inward parts, or who has granted understanding to the heart?
verses.38:37: Who can number the clouds in wisdom, or who can tilt the waterskins of heaven,
verses.38:38: when the dust hardens into a solid mass, and the clods cleave fast together?
verses.38:39: Can you hunt prey for the lioness, or fill the appetite of the young lions,
verses.38:40: when they crouch in their dens, and abide in the thicket to lie in wait?
verses.38:41: Who prepares for the raven its provision, when its young cry out to God, and wander about for lack of food?"
verses.39:1: "Do you know the time when the wild goats of the rock bring forth? Do you watch when the does travail in birth?
verses.39:2: Can you number the months that they fulfill, and do you know the time when they give birth?
verses.39:3: They bow down, they bring forth their young, and they cast off their birth pangs.
verses.39:4: Their young grow strong, they mature in the open field; they go forth and do not return to them.
verses.39:5: Who has sent the wild donkey out free? And who has loosed the bonds of the swift wild donkey,
verses.39:6: whose house I have made the wilderness, and the salt land his dwelling places?
verses.39:7: He laughs at the tumult of the city; the shouts of the driver he does not hear.
verses.39:8: He ranges the mountains as his pasture, and seeks after every green herb.
verses.39:9: Will the wild ox be willing to serve you, or will he abide through the night beside your manger?
verses.39:10: Can you bind the wild ox in the furrow with his rope, or will he harrow the valleys behind you?
verses.39:11: Will you rely upon him because his strength is great, and leave your labor to him?
verses.39:12: Will you trust him that he will bring back your grain, and gather it to your threshing floor?
verses.39:13: The wing of the ostrich waves exultantly, yet are her pinions and plumage those of the stork?
verses.39:14: For she abandons her eggs to the ground, and lets them warm in the dust,
verses.39:15: forgetting that a foot may crush them, or a wild beast of the field may trample them.
verses.39:16: She treats her young harshly, as though they were not hers; though her labor is in vain, she feels no dread,
verses.39:17: because God has deprived her of wisdom, and has not apportioned understanding to her.
verses.39:18: When she lifts herself up on high, she laughs at the horse and his rider.
verses.39:19: Do you bestow might upon the horse? Do you clothe his neck with thunder?
verses.39:20: Do you make him bound like the locust? The majesty of his snorting is terror.
verses.39:21: He paws in the valley and exults in strength; he goes forth to meet the weapons.
verses.39:22: He mocks at dread and is not dismayed, and he does not turn back before the sword.
verses.39:23: Against him the quiver rattles, the flashing spear and the javelin.
verses.39:24: With quivering and rage he swallows the ground, and he cannot stand still when the trumpet sounds.
verses.39:25: At the sound of the trumpet he cries, 'Aha!' From afar he scents the battle, the thunder of the captains and the shouting.
verses.39:26: Does the hawk take wing by your understanding, spreading his wings toward the south?
verses.39:27: Is it at your command that the eagle mounts upward, and sets his nest on high?
verses.39:28: On the rock he dwells and lodges, upon the crag of the rock and the stronghold.
verses.39:29: From there he spies out his food; from afar his eyes behold it.
verses.39:30: His young ones gulp down blood; and where the slain are, there he is."
verses.40:1: And the LORD answered Job and said,
verses.40:2: "Shall a faultfinder contend with the Almighty? Let him who reproves God answer it."
verses.40:3: Then Job answered the LORD and said,
verses.40:4: "Behold, I am of small account; what shall I reply to You? I have laid my hand upon my mouth.
verses.40:5: Once I have spoken, and I will not answer; yes, twice, and I will add no more."
verses.40:6: Then the LORD answered Job out of the tempest and said,
verses.40:7: "Gird up your loins now like a man; I will question you, and you shall make it known to Me.
verses.40:8: Will you indeed annul My justice? Will you condemn Me that you may be righteous?
verses.40:9: And do you have an arm like God, and can you thunder with a voice like His?
verses.40:10: Adorn yourself now with majesty and loftiness, and clothe yourself with glory and splendor.
verses.40:11: Pour forth the overflowings of your wrath, and look upon every proud one and bring him low.
verses.40:12: Look upon every proud one and humble him, and tread down the wicked in their place.
verses.40:13: Hide them in the dust together; bind their faces in the hidden place.
verses.40:14: Then I also will acknowledge to you that your own right hand can save you.
verses.40:15: Behold now Behemoth, which I made along with you; he eats grass like an ox.
verses.40:16: Behold now, his strength is in his loins, and his power is in the muscles of his belly.
verses.40:17: He stiffens his tail like a cedar; the sinews of his thighs are knit tightly together.
verses.40:18: His bones are tubes of bronze; his limbs are like bars of iron.
verses.40:19: He is the foremost of the ways of God; let Him who made him bring near His sword.
verses.40:20: Surely the mountains bring forth produce for him, and all the beasts of the field play there.
verses.40:21: He lies beneath the lotus trees, in the covert of the reed and the marsh.
verses.40:22: The lotus trees cover him with shade; the willows of the brook surround him.
verses.40:23: Behold, though a river surges violently, he is not alarmed; he remains confident though the Jordan rushes against his mouth.
verses.40:24: Can anyone capture him while he watches, or pierce his nose with snares?
verses.40:25: Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook, or press down his tongue with a cord?
verses.40:26: Can you put a rush cord through his nose, or pierce his jaw with a hook?
verses.40:27: Will he make many supplications to you? Will he speak gentle words to you?
verses.40:28: Will he make a covenant with you? Will you take him for a servant forever?
verses.40:29: Will you play with him as with a bird, or bind him for your maidens?
verses.40:30: Will partners bargain over him? Will they divide him among the merchants?
verses.40:31: Can you fill his skin with harpoons, or his head with fishing spears?
verses.40:32: Lay your hand upon him; remember the battle—you will not do it again."
verses.41:1: "Behold, any hope concerning him is in vain; is one not cast down even at the sight of him?
verses.41:2: No one is so fierce that he dares to stir him up; who then is able to stand before Me?
verses.41:3: Who has first given to Me, that I should repay him? All that is under the whole heaven is Mine.
verses.41:4: Concerning him, shall I keep silent about his limbs, or the matter of his mighty power, or the grace of his frame?
verses.41:5: Who can strip off the face of his outer covering? Who can enter within his double bridle?
verses.41:6: Who can open the doors of his face? All around his teeth is terror.
verses.41:7: Rows of shields are his pride, shut up closely as with a tight seal.
verses.41:8: One lies so close to another that no air can pass between them.
verses.41:9: They are joined one to another; they interlock and cannot be separated.
verses.41:10: His sneezings flash forth light, and his eyes are like the eyelids of the dawn.
verses.41:11: Out of his mouth proceed flaming torches; sparks of fire leap forth.
verses.41:12: Out of his nostrils goes forth smoke, as from a boiling pot and burning rushes.
verses.41:13: His breath kindles coals, and a flame goes forth from his mouth.
verses.41:14: Strength abides in his neck, and dismay dances before him.
verses.41:15: The folds of his flesh cleave tightly together; they are cast firm upon him and cannot be moved.
verses.41:16: His heart is cast hard as a stone, yes, cast hard as a lower millstone.
verses.41:17: When he rises up, the mighty are terrified; because of his crashings, they lose their bearings.
verses.41:18: Though the sword reaches him, it cannot prevail, nor the spear, the dart, or the javelin.
verses.41:19: He counts iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood.
verses.41:20: The arrow cannot put him to flight; slingstones are turned into stubble for him.
verses.41:21: Clubs are regarded as stubble, and he laughs at the rattling of the javelin.
verses.41:22: His underparts are sharp potsherds; he spreads himself like a threshing sledge upon the mire.
verses.41:23: He causes the deep to boil like a pot; he makes the sea like a cauldron of ointment.
verses.41:24: Behind him he makes a shining wake; one would think the deep to be white-haired.
verses.41:25: Upon the earth there is none like him, one made without fear.
verses.41:26: He looks upon every lofty thing; he is king over all the sons of pride."
verses.42:1: And Job answered the LORD and said,
verses.42:2: "I know that You are able to do all things, and that no purpose can be restrained from You.
verses.42:3: 'Who is this who conceals counsel without knowledge?' Therefore I have declared what I did not comprehend, things too wondrous for me, which I did not know.
verses.42:4: 'Listen now, and I will speak; I will ask you, and you shall inform Me.'
verses.42:5: By the hearing of the ear I had heard of You, but now my eye has seen You.
verses.42:6: Therefore I loathe myself, and I repent in dust and ashes."
verses.42:7: Now it came to pass, after the LORD had spoken these words to Job, that the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite, "My wrath is kindled against you and against your two companions, for you have not spoken concerning Me what is right, as My servant Job has.
verses.42:8: And now, take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to My servant Job, and offer up a burnt offering on your behalf; and My servant Job shall pray for you, for him I will surely accept, lest I deal with you according to your folly, because you have not spoken concerning Me what is right, as My servant Job has."
verses.42:9: So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did as the LORD had spoken to them; and the LORD accepted Job.
verses.42:10: And the LORD restored the fortunes of Job when he prayed for his friends, and the LORD increased all that belonged to Job twofold.
verses.42:11: Then all his brothers, and all his sisters, and all who had known him formerly came to him and ate bread with him in his house; and they grieved with him and comforted him over all the calamity that the LORD had brought upon him. And each one gave him a piece of silver, and each one a ring of gold.
verses.42:12: And the LORD blessed the latter years of Job more than his beginning, and he had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, one thousand yoke of oxen, and one thousand female donkeys.
verses.42:13: And he had seven sons and three daughters.
verses.42:14: He called the name of the first Jemimah, and the name of the second Keziah, and the name of the third Keren-Happuch.
verses.42:15: And no women were found so fair as the daughters of Job in all the land; and their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.
verses.42:16: And Job lived after this one hundred and forty years, and he saw his children and his children's children, four generations.
verses.42:17: And Job died, aged and full of days.

notes.1:5: Cursed translates a Hebrew verb literally meaning blessed, a reverent euphemism used here and in 1:11, 2:5, and 2:9 to avoid placing the word curse directly beside God.
notes.1:6: Satan translates the Hebrew title meaning the Adversary or the Accuser, who appears in the heavenly council among the sons of God.
notes.1:10: Translated according to the Masoretic Qere reading the full spelling of the masculine pronoun you; the Ketiv preserves a shorter orthographic spelling with the same meaning.
notes.2:7: Translated according to the Masoretic Qere reading even to with the conjunction; the Ketiv omits the conjunction and reads simply to.
notes.2:9: As in 1:5, curse translates a Hebrew euphemism literally meaning bless to avoid speaking a direct curse against God.
notes.2:10: Adversity renders the Hebrew noun that can mean evil or calamity, referring here to affliction and misfortune rather than moral wickedness.
notes.3:1: His day refers idiomatically to the day of Job's birth, as unfolded in 3:3.
notes.3:6: Rejoice follows the Masoretic vocalization of the Hebrew verb; a different vocalization of the same consonants yields be joined or be united.
notes.3:8: Leviathan is a formidable sea creature of biblical poetic imagery representing untamed cosmic chaos (compare Job 41 and Psalm 74:14).
notes.3:10: My mother's womb renders the concise Hebrew idiom literally reading my womb, meaning the womb that bore Job.
notes.4:17: The Hebrew preposition min in me-Eloah and me-osehu may be read either as "before God" and "before his Maker" or comparatively as "more righteous than God" and "purer than his Maker."
notes.4:18: The Hebrew noun toholah occurs only here in the Old Testament and denotes "error" or "folly."
notes.4:21: Hebrew yitram means "their tent cord" (matching the verb "plucked up" and the dwelling imagery of verse 19), though it can also be understood as "their excellence" or "abundance."
notes.5:5: Following the Masoretic vocalization tsammim, the noun signifies "a snare" (cf. Job 18:9); ancient versions and some commentators revocalize it to mean "the thirsty."
notes.5:7: Hebrew bene-resheph, literally "sons of flame," is a poetic idiom for rising sparks.
notes.5:24: Hebrew lo techeta, literally "you shall not miss," expresses here the concrete sense of finding nothing missing when inspecting one's dwelling.
notes.6:2: The translation follows the qere reading meaning 'and my calamity'; the ketiv preserves an older orthographic spelling of the same word.
notes.6:6: The rare Hebrew phrase traditionally rendered 'the white of an egg' is also understood by some lexicons as the bland juice of the purslane or mallow plant.
notes.6:29: The translation follows the qere plural imperative 'and turn again' addressed to Job's friends, rather than the ketiv spelling.
notes.7:1: The translation follows the qere poetic preposition 'upon' rather than the shorter prose ketiv spelling, with no difference in meaning.
notes.7:5: The translation follows the qere reading 'and crusts of dust' (literally clods of dust); the ketiv reflects an orthographic variant of the same noun.
notes.7:20: The Masoretic text reads 'to myself,' which ancient scribal tradition lists among the Tiqqune Soferim as a reverent substitution for 'to You.'
notes.8:11: Hebrew gome denotes the papyrus plant and achu refers to marsh reed grass, both of which depend entirely on standing water to thrive.
notes.8:17: The Hebrew verb translated "looks upon" literally means "sees," picturing the plant spreading across and resting upon a stony foundation.
notes.8:18: The verb "is destroyed" is an indefinite active form in Hebrew, literally "if one swallows him up from his place."
notes.9:9: The Hebrew names Ash, Kesil, and Kimah denote constellations traditionally identified as the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades, while "the chambers of the south" refers to the stars of the southern hemisphere.
notes.9:13: Rahab is a poetic Hebrew name for a mythical sea monster symbolizing proud, rebellious power subdued beneath God.
notes.9:19: Translated according to the Masoretic Hebrew first-person suffix ("appoint a time for me"); some ancient versions read a third-person suffix ("summon Him").
notes.9:26: "Skiffs of reed" renders Hebrew oniyyot eveh, light papyrus boats renowned in antiquity for their speed.
notes.9:30: Translated according to the Masoretic Qere ("with snow water"); the Ketiv reads "in snow."
notes.10:15: The Hebrew form rendered 'beholding' may be read either as a verbal adjective parallel to 'sated' or as an imperative addressed to God, 'behold my affliction.'
notes.10:17: The phrase 'relays and a warring host' reflects the Hebrew hendiadys for waves of fresh troops arrayed in succession against Job.
notes.10:20: Follows the qere imperatives 'cease' and 'turn away'; the ketiv reads third-person verb forms, 'let it cease' and 'let Him turn away.'
notes.10:22: The Hebrew term translated 'the shadow of death' denotes deepest gloom, and the final clause literally reads 'and it shines forth like thick darkness.'
notes.11:6: The Hebrew verb rendered 'exacts of you less than' comes from a root meaning 'to forget' or 'to remit,' expressing that God overlooks part of Job's iniquity.
notes.11:12: The Hebrew pairs a wordplay between 'empty-headed' (literally 'hollow') and 'gain understanding' (literally 'acquire a heart') with a proverb of impossibility.
notes.11:17: The word translated 'darkness' denotes dense gloom, contrasting sharply with the bright morning promised upon repentance.
notes.12:5: Translated according to the Masoretic vocalization meaning 'a lamp' or 'torch'; an alternative consonantal division yields 'contempt for misfortune.'
notes.12:6: The final clause is compact in Hebrew and may mean either 'those who carry their god in their own hand' (trusting in their own might) or 'those into whose hand God brings provision.'
notes.12:9: This is the sole occurrence of the covenant name 'the LORD' in the poetic dialogues of Job, where the titles 'God' and 'the Almighty' otherwise predominate.
notes.13:12: The Hebrew word rendered 'bulwarks' literally denotes mounds or shield-bosses, used figuratively here for fragile arguments or defenses.
notes.13:15: The ketiv reads 'not' ('I have no hope' or 'I will not wait'), whereas the qere, followed here, reads 'in Him' ('in Him I will hope').
notes.13:27: Literally 'the roots of my feet,' referring to the soles or footprints of one closely confined and watched.
notes.14:3: The Masoretic Text reads 'me,' shifting directly from mortal humanity in general to Job's own trial before God.
notes.14:13: Sheol is the Hebrew term for the subterranean realm of the dead.
notes.14:14: The Hebrew terms for 'appointed service' and 'relief' draw on the imagery of hard military duty and the awaited replacement of a soldier on watch.
notes.14:16: The second clause may be read as a rhetorical question depicting Job's present distress, or as continuing the wish of verses thirteen through fifteen ('For then You would count my steps; You would not keep watch over my sin').
notes.15:12: The Hebrew verb rendered "flash" occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and denotes winking, blinking, or flashing the eyes in indignation or arrogance.
notes.15:22: Follows the Masoretic Qere (passive participle, "watched for" or "awaited"); the Ketiv reflects an active or defective form.
notes.15:29: The rare Hebrew noun rendered "their possessions" is a hapax legomenon whose exact sense is uncertain, traditionally understood as property, wealth, or grain-ears; the third-person plural suffix shifts briefly to the wicked collectively.
notes.15:30: "His mouth" refers to God, whose sovereign breath sweeps away the wicked (compare Isaiah 11:4).
notes.16:7: The Hebrew shifts abruptly within the verse from speaking about God in the third person ("He has worn me out") to addressing Him directly in the second person ("You have made desolate").
notes.16:16: Follows the Masoretic Qere (plural verb, agreeing grammatically with the plural noun "face"); the Ketiv reads a feminine singular verb form.
notes.16:19: The word rendered "my advocate" is an Aramaizing term meaning "my witness" (parallel to the standard Hebrew word for witness in the first line).
notes.17:3: Striking hands was the ancient gesture of legally guaranteeing a debt or standing as surety for another.
notes.17:5: This terse proverb speaks literally of informing against friends for a share or portion, warning that such treachery brings ruin upon one's own children.
notes.17:16: The Hebrew word rendered "rest" can also be taken as a verb meaning "descend," yielding "Shall we go down together into the dust?"
notes.18:13: "The firstborn of death" is a poetic personification of the deadliest disease or most fatal affliction.
notes.18:20: The Hebrew terms for "those in the west" and "those in the east" literally mean those behind and those before, and may alternatively denote succeeding and preceding generations.
notes.19:17: "The children of my own body" renders a Hebrew idiom meaning "sons of my womb" or "body," referring here to Job's uterine brothers or close household kin.
notes.19:25: "Redeemer" translates the Hebrew goel, the kinsman-redeemer or legal vindicator who defends the rights and honor of a wronged relative.
notes.19:26: The Hebrew preposition in "from my flesh" can signify either "from within my flesh" or "apart from my flesh"; the opening clause is literally "after my skin, they have struck off this."
notes.19:28: The Masoretic text reads first-person "in me" rather than "in him," reflecting Job's vivid shift from reporting his friends' words into his own perspective.
notes.19:29: The qere reads a rare noun form meaning "that there is a judgment," differing slightly in spelling from the ketiv's more common noun form with the same sense.
notes.20:23: The Hebrew word rendered "as his food" can also mean "into his flesh" or "while he eats."
notes.20:26: The Hebrew verb rendered "shall consume" may also be understood as "it shall go ill with" whoever remains in his tent.
notes.20:29: Literally "the heritage of his word," meaning the destiny decreed or appointed for him by God.
notes.21:13: Following the Masoretic qere ("they finish" or "complete"); the ketiv reads "they wear out" or "spend."
notes.21:19: The opening clause is widely understood as Job citing his friends' own argument before rebutting it in the second half of the verse.
notes.21:24: The rare Hebrew term rendered "his pails" is uncertain and is alternatively understood by some interpreters as "his body" or "his sides."
notes.21:30: The Hebrew phrasing may mean either that the wicked man is "spared in" the day of calamity or that he is "reserved for" it; the former fits the flow of Job's argument in verses 29 through 33.
notes.22:17: The Masoretic Hebrew shifts from first-person plural ("from us") to third-person plural ("to them") within the quoted speech of the wicked.
notes.22:25: The Hebrew noun echoes the word for precious gold or gold ore in verse twenty-four, creating a wordplay that presents the Almighty Himself as Job's true treasure.
notes.22:30: The expression "one who is not innocent" translates a rare Hebrew negative prefix found also in the name Ichabod.
notes.23:2: The Hebrew word rendered "bitter" literally denotes rebellion or defiance, and the Masoretic reading "my hand" is preserved faithfully rather than following the Septuagint's "His hand."
notes.23:12: "More than my allotted portion" translates the Masoretic Hebrew literally, referring to one's prescribed daily portion or necessary food.
notes.23:13: "Unchangeable" translates the Hebrew phrase literally meaning "in one," expressing God's solitary, unalterable singleness of purpose.
notes.24:6: Ketiv/Qere: the written consonantal text (ketiv) reads a form suggesting "they cause to reap," whereas the traditional read text (qere) translated here reads the standard Qal verb "they reap."
notes.24:12: The Masoretic vocalization reads "men" rather than "the dying," and is followed directly here.
notes.24:22: The Hebrew verb rendered "drags away" can also mean "prolongs," and the final word for "life" displays an Aramaizing plural ending characteristic of Job's poetry.
notes.25:3: "Hosts" renders Hebrew gedudim, denoting military troops or heavenly armies marshaled under God's command.
notes.25:5: The rare Hebrew verb ya'ahil means "to shine" or "to give brightness," emphasizing that even the most luminous heavenly bodies appear dim before God's purity.
notes.26:4: The Hebrew phrase 'et-mi may be understood either as "To whom" or "With whose help," ironically questioning the source of Bildad's speech.
notes.26:5: "The shades of the dead" translates Hebrew rephaim, referring to the departed spirits inhabiting the underworld beneath the cosmic waters.
notes.26:6: "Abaddon" means "Destruction" and stands in poetic parallel with Sheol as a designation for the realm of the dead.
notes.26:12: Translates the Masoretic Qere ubitvunato ("and by His understanding") rather than the Ketiv spelling ubetovanto. The verb raga' can mean either "stilled" or "stirred up," and "Rahab" denotes a primordial sea monster symbolizing chaotic pride subdued by God.
notes.27:8: The Hebrew verb yivtsa' can mean either "when he is cut off" or "though he gains dishonest wealth," highlighting the futility of the godless when God claims his life.
notes.27:15: "Buried by death" reflects the Masoretic idiom bammawet, where "death" often denotes deadly pestilence leaving survivors without honorable burial or mourning.
notes.27:19: Follows the Masoretic Hebrew lo' ye'asef ("will not be gathered," meaning denied honorable burial or gathering to his fathers), whereas some ancient versions read "will do so no more."
notes.27:22: The grammatical subject in verses 22 and 23 continues the personified east wind from verse 21, though some interpreters understand the verbs impersonally or as referring to divine judgment.
notes.28:4: Describes ancient miners descending deep shafts far from settled habitation, hanging suspended on ropes as they work in the dark.
notes.28:18: The Hebrew word rendered "acquisition" literally means a "drawing out" or "pouch," signifying either the gaining of wisdom or its price.
notes.28:22: Abaddon is a Hebrew term meaning "Destruction," used here as a poetic personification of the realm of the dead.
notes.29:4: "Prime" translates the Hebrew word for "autumn," the harvest season used figuratively for the fruitful maturity of Job's former life; "intimate counsel" denotes close, trusted fellowship.
notes.29:18: The Hebrew word rendered "sand" is a common emblem of vast abundance, though an ancient Jewish tradition also interprets it as the legendary phoenix in light of the parallel mention of a "nest."
notes.29:24: The clause "they did not believe it" may indicate either that they could scarcely believe Job's gracious favor or that he smiled upon them to reassure them when they lacked confidence.
notes.30:11: The read form (Qere) has "my bowstring" or "my cord," while the written form (Ketiv) has "His bowstring"; both convey that God has stripped Job of strength and opened him to humiliation.
notes.30:22: The read form (Qere) is tushiyyah, meaning "substance," "security," or "soundness," whereas the written form (Ketiv) is commonly understood as "storm" or "crashing tempest."
notes.30:24: The Hebrew phrasing is terse and difficult; it may depict a ruined person instinctively reaching out for help in disaster, or affirm that one does not strike a heap of ruins when it cries out.
notes.31:11: The read form (Qere) aligns the gender of each pronoun with its predicate noun, "heinous wickedness" and "iniquity," whereas the written form (Ketiv) reverses their genders.
notes.31:12: Hebrew Abaddon means "Destruction" and is used poetically in Job for the realm of ruin and the grave.
notes.31:33: The Hebrew phrase translated "as Adam did" may refer specifically to the first man hiding his sin in Genesis 3, or more generally "as mortals do."
notes.32:9: Hebrew rabbim can mean either the great or those of many years, standing in parallel with the aged in the second line.
notes.32:19: New wineskins refers to freshly filled skins strained to the bursting point by newly fermenting wine.
notes.32:21: Show partiality translates the Hebrew idiom lift up the face of a man; give flattering titles renders a verb meaning to address with honorific surnames.
notes.33:6: Pinched out renders a rare verb describing a potter pinching off a portion of clay to form a vessel.
notes.33:19: Following the qere (read form), the multitude of his bones; the ketiv (written form) reads the strife of his bones.
notes.33:21: Following the qere (read form), are laid bare (or protrude); the ketiv (written form) reads the noun bareness.
notes.33:27: The verb looks upon follows the Masoretic vocalization from the root meaning to behold; others connect it with the verb to sing (he sings before men).
notes.33:28: Following the qere (read form), third-person his soul and his life; the ketiv (written form) reads first-person my soul and my life, continuing the direct confession of verse 27.
notes.34:6: Hebrew literally reads "my arrow," used by metonymy for the wound inflicted by an arrow.
notes.34:18: The Masoretic Text uses an interrogative infinitive ("Should one say"), arguing from the respect owed to earthly rulers to the far greater reverence owed to God.
notes.34:23: The Hebrew reads "further" or "again," indicating that God has no need to prolong His examination before bringing a person to judgment.
notes.34:36: The opening Hebrew word is a rare exclamation meaning "Oh, that!" or "My desire is."
notes.35:2: Hebrew literally reads "my righteousness more than God," expressing Elihu's charge that Job claims to be more righteous than God.
notes.35:3: The Hebrew shifts abruptly from second person ("to you") to first person ("shall I gain"), and literally reads "from my sin," meaning "more than if I had sinned."
notes.35:15: The Hebrew noun rendered "arrogance" occurs only here in the Old Testament and is variously understood as "arrogance," "transgression," or "folly."
notes.36:14: Hebrew qedeshim denotes male cult prostitutes associated with pagan shrine practices, symbolizing a life wasted and cut short in moral ruin.
notes.36:18: The Hebrew wording is terse; the noun safeq can refer either to a chastising blow or to derisive hand-clapping and scoffing.
notes.36:30: Hebrew or literally means light and is used in this storm passage (36:30, 32; 37:3, 11, 15) for lightning; "roots of the sea" poetically denotes the ocean's deepest foundations.
notes.36:33: Following the Masoretic Text, "Its thunder" (re'o, roar) announces God's coming in the storm, and even the livestock sense what is rising (oleh).
notes.37:6: Literally "Be upon the earth," using an Aramaizing imperative form of the verb "to be" to command the snow to fall.
notes.37:9: "Its chamber" refers to the storehouse of the southern tempest (compare 9:9), and "the scattering winds" (mezarim) denote the cold northern winds that disperse clouds.
notes.37:20: The Hebrew forms a double rhetorical question underscoring the danger of demanding an audience with God; the second clause may also be read conditionally, "If a man speaks, surely he will be swallowed up."
notes.37:24: The verse closes Elihu's speech with a Hebrew wordplay between "fear Him" (yere'uhu) and "has no regard" (lo-yir'eh, literally "does not look upon").
notes.38:1: The ketiv writes the preposition and noun as a single word, while the qere separates them as min hasearah, translated here as from the whirlwind.
notes.38:12: The qere supplies the definite article before dawn and uses the standard second-person verb spelling, whereas the ketiv omits the article and appends a final he to the verb.
notes.38:32: Mazzaroth is a transliteration of a rare Hebrew astronomical term referring to a prominent constellation or the constellations of the zodiac in their seasonal circuit.
notes.38:36: The rare Hebrew words translated inward parts and heart follow traditional interpretation; some scholars alternatively understand them as cloud layers and celestial signs or weather-sensing birds.
notes.39:5: The two Hebrew terms rendered wild donkey and swift wild donkey are poetic synonyms designating the untamed desert onager.
notes.39:12: The translation follows the qere, a transitive Hiphil verb meaning to bring back, whereas the ketiv reads the intransitive Qal form meaning to return.
notes.39:13: The Hebrew noun for stork derives from the root for kindness or devotion, creating an intentional contrast between the stork's maternal care and the ostrich's harshness toward her young.
notes.39:19: The Hebrew term rendered thunder literally evokes quivering or thunderous motion and is also widely understood to describe the warhorse's flowing, trembling mane.
notes.40:6: The Ketiv writes the preposition and noun as a single word, while the Masoretic Qere divides them into two words, min se'arah, meaning out of the tempest or whirlwind.
notes.40:15: Behemoth is an intensive plural of the Hebrew word for beast, designating a creature of immense size and strength.
notes.40:19: The clause literally reads He who made him brings near His sword, indicating that only God can master Behemoth, though some understand it of God equipping the creature with its own weapon.
notes.40:25: Masoretic verses 40:25 through 40:32 correspond to 41:1 through 41:8 in most English versifications; Leviathan denotes a fearsome sea creature.
notes.41:4: The Masoretic Qere reads lo, meaning concerning him or for him, rendered here as a rhetorical question; the Ketiv reads lo with an alef, meaning not, yielding I will not keep silent concerning his limbs.
notes.41:5: The expression double bridle literally renders kefel risno and refers poetically to Leviathan's formidable double jaws or layered armor.
notes.41:17: The Hebrew elim denotes the mighty or heavenly beings, and the verb yitchatta'u means to lose one's bearings or shrink back in terror.
notes.41:26: Sons of pride renders bene shachats, an idiom for the proudest and fiercest wild creatures.
notes.42:2: The ketiv omits the final yod (potentially a defective spelling or second-person form), whereas the qere reads the first-person form "I know."
notes.42:4: In verses three and four, Job cites the LORD's own earlier summons to him (Job 38:2-3; 40:7) before answering in humility.
notes.42:6: The Hebrew verb translated "loathe" lacks an explicit object; it is traditionally understood reflexively ("loathe myself") or as referring to Job's earlier words ("retract").
notes.42:10: The ketiv reads "shevit" and the qere reads "shevut," variant forms of the noun in the Hebrew idiom meaning "to restore the fortunes" or "turn the captivity."
notes.42:16: The ketiv preserves the shorter verb form and the qere the fuller spelling, both conveying "and he saw."
